title: Prithu asks for ten thousand ears
hook: a king offered any boon turns down liberation
carry: pure bhakti makes even liberation look light
tomorrow: a mother's rope keeps coming up two fingers short. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the priests' wives, and the definition in Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: pure bhakti is love with nothing laid on top. Today, a line that sounds backwards, and a king who lived it.

In the Bhagavata Purana, King Prithu has just come through a bitter quarrel with Indra, king of the gods, over a stolen sacrificial horse. The quarrel is calmed, and Vishnu himself arrives, with Indra beside him, and stands before Prithu, pleased. Ask for a boon, he says. Here's what makes the story famous. Prithu doesn't ask for a longer reign or a safer kingdom. He doesn't even ask for moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death, which many Hindu schools name the goal past every goal. In paraphrase he says: I don't want even that liberation, if there's no hearing about you in it. Give me ten thousand ears. Why would anyone turn down the finish line?
screen: `ASK FOR A BOON.` → `NOT EVEN LIBERATION.` → `GIVE ME TEN THOUSAND EARS.`

segments.voice: Rupa answers in his list of what pure bhakti does. In paraphrase: it ends suffering. It brings what is good. It makes liberation seem light. It is very hard to come by. It is a joy that is dense and of a special kind. And it draws Krishna himself. The first marks are what anyone might hope from a spiritual path. Then the turn. A devotee who has tasted that dense joy isn't looking for the exit, because the exit was never the prize. The love is. That's Prithu's ten thousand ears: he'd rather keep hearing about Vishnu forever than be finished. The Bhagavata says it again elsewhere: the Lord, teaching as the sage Kapila, speaks of devotees who won't accept liberation, even when it's offered, if it comes without serving him. And the last mark is the boldest. Bhakti doesn't only carry the devotee toward God. In this lineage, love pulls God toward the devotee. This is a real fork in Hindu thought. For many schools, moksha stays the highest aim, and later this week the track hears one of them, with Shankara. Rupa's book says plainly where it stands. Gaudiya devotees pray for loving service, life after life, not for the exit.
screen: `ENDS SUFFERING, BRINGS GOOD.` · `PRITHU'S EARS: NOT THE EXIT.` · `IT DRAWS KRISHNA HIMSELF.` · then, large: `SERVICE, LIFE AFTER LIFE.`

segments.voice: Put on one devotional song, a bhajan or a kirtan your family plays, or hum one you remember, and give it the whole of your hearing, with nothing else open. If you pray, let it be Prithu's prayer: one more hearing. If you don't, just notice the moment you stop waiting for it to end.
Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book that lists what pure bhakti does, up to making liberation seem light and drawing Krishna close.

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava teaching, these marks of pure bhakti are read as signs to recognize, and devotees speak of loving service, not liberation, as what they hope for. Hearing Krishna's stories and singing his names together is a central daily practice.

sources.ref: Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.1.17 (the marks of pure bhakti: ends suffering, gives good, makes liberation light, very rare, dense joy, draws Krishna)
